global: The field was ours by right, yet {player} has taken it with trickery. A cheap victory is still a defeat for honour.
Let the chroniclers record that {player} won the field with {troop_count} men. I shall remember the number, and the debt.
Another day, another smug banner raised on my ground. {player} may gloat now; the ledger is not closed.
Ser {player} rode over my line like a farmer's cart over a rut. I shall not forget the jolt.
Hark, all Ormerath: {player} calls a bloody trampling a glorious fight. Let the minstrels write the truth instead.
Those {troop_count} soldiers of mine died cursing the mud, not the enemy. Their blood will be paid for.
I lost the field to {player}, damn it all. Enjoy the mud you so proudly stood in, friend.
A wise lord knows when to withdraw, and I withdrew only because {player} outnumbered my patience.
Ser {player}, your victory smells of a hired mercenary's luck. Bring a true army next time and we shall see.
Mark this day: {player} took the field, and I took a vow. The next meeting will not end in a mere skirmish.
whisper: You beat my line today, ser {player}, but a bitter winner sleeps poorly. I will be waiting at dawn.
Enjoy your ill-earned field. Every drop of my men's sweat is a coin I intend to collect from you.
Do not mistake one muddy field for the whole war, ser {player}. The war is long and I have patience.
I expected a fair contest and got a sneak attack from {player}. Remember that I notice such things.
I counted the steps from my ruined line to your banner. Soon I will walk them the other way.
Gloat in your tent tonight, ser {player}. Tomorrow I will be the one sharpening my blade.
The ground you took was soaked by {troop_count} of my sworn men. Do not ask me to forgive that.
Your trick at the ford was clever, I grant it. Clever men are sometimes hanged, and I know the rope.
Ser {player}, I am not bitter about the field. I am bitter that you smiled while my standard fell.
Keep your victory close, for I am already drafting the letter that will undo it. Expect a visitor.
face: So it is you, ser {player}. You won the field, and I would sooner eat my own shield than say well done.
Hold there. You have trampled my ground and mocked my dead. Pass on quickly, before I forget my honour.
You stand over my fallen banner with a grin, ser {player}. Enjoy it while the mud still holds your boots.
Ah, the victor of the morning. My men are still picking thorns from their legs because of your charge.
I will not bow to a sworn noble who fights like a thief in the night. Speak your business, then be gone.
A fine day for you, I suppose. Those {troop_count} men who fell here would not agree, but they cannot speak.
Your smile offends me more than your spears did. Walk on, ser {player}, and think on how close the next fight will be.
I hear the minstrels already sing of your charge. Let them sing; I shall sing of the knife I keep for you.
We meet again on the road, and you carry the taste of a won field. Take care, for good luck does not last forever.
Begone from my sight, ser {player}. I am too proud to strike you while you ride with your victory.

global: The field went to {player} today. It is a fair result, though the wind was not in my favour.
Last morning's clash ended as the scales dictated. Ser {player} held the ground; I shall reckon the losses and move on.
A defeat, certainly, but not the end of the saga. The banners of my house still fly and the roads are open.
Ser {player} has the field and the glory of it. I have the lesson, and lessons cost less than pride.
The mud at the ford has kept a fine record of the morning. Ser {player} wrote the last line of it.
I lost the field to {player} with {troop_count} men standing. The rest will regroup under my own command.
Let all the realm note: a battle was fought, a battle was lost, and ale will be served at the next gathering.
Honour holds even in defeat. Ser {player} fought well enough, and I expect the same courtesy next time.
The lines broke near the old mill. The story of it will be told by those who survived, which is not me.
Fortune favoured the other banner this day. I shall study its tactics, then see who laughs last.
whisper: The field was yours this day, ser {player}. I will not pretend otherwise, nor will I pretend to be pleased.
A quick word: your flank was well chosen. I noted it, and I expect to see it again.
I am not angry, merely tired. A lost field is a long ride home, and you rode it faster than I did.
Do not expect a letter of complaint from me, ser {player}. Defeat is a teacher, and I am a diligent pupil.
Your banners held the mill while mine broke. Remember that luck can turn; it turned on me this time.
We fought, you prevailed, and now there is ale to be shared. Come find me if you care to talk.
I have sent word to my steward about the losses. The accounts will be settled, one way or another, in time.
Ser {player}, I will be frank: the terrain favoured you. Let us speak of it when the dust has settled.
The field is yours, so take what honour it carries. I have no need of it at present.
Our meeting at the ford was cordial enough. Let us keep it that way, for the realm has enough enemies.
face: Good morning, ser {player}. You hold the field I lost. Pass if your business is peaceful, and I shall pass as well.
Ah, you again. I have nothing to say about the battle except that it is over and the mud is terrible.
I see your banners by the mill. Keep to the road and we will have no trouble, ser {player}.
Hold a moment, traveller. My men are weary and my pride is bruised. State your purpose quickly, if you please.
You fought well enough, I suppose. Let us not make the afternoon longer by quarrelling over the morning.
The field is yours, ser {player}. The road beyond it is not, and I would like to cross it in peace.
We have met before on a battlefield. Today we meet on a road, which is a more civil place to speak.
I carry the loss of {troop_count} men on my back. Do not add to it with a boast, and we shall part well.
Ser {player}, your men hold the ford now. I have no quarrel with you for that, only with the weather.
Greetings. A lost battle makes a sober companion, and I am quite sober. What brings you across my path?

global: Ser {player} carried the field with courage this morning. My defeat is lighter knowing a worthy hand took it.
Let it be spoken: I lost the field to {player}, and I would lose to no one else with more pleasure.
The banners fell today, but a friend's banner rose in their place. Praise the ancestors for a sporting foe.
Well fought, ser {player}. The ford will remember your charge and so will I, with a grin rather than a grudge.
I bow to the victor of the morning. Ser {player} outmatched my lines, and my heart is glad for it.
We lost {troop_count} men this day, yet the honour of the contest was shared. Ser {player}, you have my respect.
A glorious rout, though I was on the wrong end of it. May the next field be ours to share in better fortune.
Ser {player}, the minstrels will sing of this charge for a generation. I will be the first to hum along.
Defeat by a friend is a lesser sorrow. I shall toast your victory at the hearth tonight, ser.
The mud is cold, but the company is warm. Ser {player} wins the day, and I count the loss a fair price for such a fight.
whisper: You bested me fairly at the mill, ser {player}. I would rather lose to you than win against a coward.
The field is yours, and I am happy for you. Come share a cup, friend, and tell me how you did it.
I was beaten, but I enjoyed every moment of the chase. Your flanking move was beautiful to behold.
Do not gloat too much, ser {player}, or I shall challenge you to a rematch with a grin on my face.
A good loss is still a good story. Yours will be the next tale I tell by the fire, if you allow it.
You have my blessing for the victory. Keep the banner high, and keep your honour higher still.
My men are grumbling, but I told them the field went to someone worthy. That someone is you.
Ser {player}, whatever you do next, I hope it brings you as much glory as today. Fare well and ride safe.
Your victory warms me more than my loss chills me. Let us meet soon and drink to the next contest.
I shall write to my kin of your charge. They will want to know whom I lost to, and why I was glad of it.
face: Ser {player}! I hoped I would meet you on this road. You beat me well, and I cannot say I mind it much.
Hail, friend. The field was yours, but the afternoon is ours. Shall we ride together to the hall tonight?
Look at you, ser {player}, looking like the victor of a hundred songs. Well done, and do not let it go to your head.
I was bested at the ford, and I am glad of it. Come, let us share some bread and tell the tale properly.
Ser {player}, your charge this morning was a sight to see. My men still speak of it, and of your steady hand.
We lost {troop_count} men to your banner, but the ground was honourably taken. Go with honour, ser, and rest well.
A kind welcome to you, ser {player}. The field is yours, the wine is mine, and I wish to pour it for you.
You have my respect, traveller. Let no one tell you the morning was anything but a fair contest between friends.
Ah, my worthy foe! I lost to you today, and I would gladly lose again just to see you smile this way.
Speak freely, ser {player}. The lines are behind us and the road is open. Shall we walk awhile together?
